Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01832
According to the first, Jahm allowed that God might know all things before they exist through a kind of knowledge that God brings into being before them.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01833
But al-Ashʿarī then reports another account that says the opposite:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01834

“Someone else reported the opposite from him, claiming that God knows a thing at the moment it comes into existence. It is impossible for a thing to be known while it does not exist”—that is, before it comes into being—“because for Jahm, a ‘thing’ is an existing body. What does not exist is not a thing, and therefore cannot be known or unknown.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01835

When we compare this second account with what al-Shahrastānī reports, and with the similar accounts found in al-Baghdādī and al-Ṣafadī, there is good reason to think that Jahm believed God’s knowledge of a thing arises when the thing itself comes into existence, not before.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01836
But our main concern here is not to settle historically which of these two positions Jahm actually held.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01837
What matters most is the way he thought about the problem and tried to solve it.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01838

From the statements attributed to him by the major historians of the Islamic schools, we can see that this determinist thinker relied on a rational method very close to philosophical reasoning. Even when dealing with these metaphysical questions, he worked with abstract concepts.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01839
There is, however, a contradiction in Jahm’s thought.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01840
It appears in the tension between his determinism and his strong insistence on denying knowledge as an eternal attribute of God.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01841

If God has no prior knowledge of human actions that will happen later, then those actions are not known to Him in advance. They therefore cannot be governed in advance by divine will. At that point, determinism falls away and human choice returns.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01841
6 — The Question of Faith
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01842
Here we find another development beyond the way the Khārijites had treated this question earlier.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01843
For most Muslims, the usual understanding of faith had two parts: first, belief in God and His messengers; and second, openly declaring that belief.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01844
The Khārijites then added a third element: acting according to that belief. In their view, there could be no true faith unless belief and profession were joined by action.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01845
With Jahm, however, the meaning of faith takes on a new form.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01846
He reduces it to a single new element: knowledge.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01847
Faith, in Jahm’s view, means knowing God, His messengers, and everything that comes from God. Nothing else counts as faith.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01848
Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī describes Jahm’s doctrine in these words:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01849

“Faith is knowledge alone. Everything apart from knowledge—professing it with the tongue, submitting and surrendering to God and His Messenger, honoring them, fearing them, and performing acts with the body—is not faith.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01850
Al-Shahrastānī gives Jahm’s position in another form:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01851
“If someone gains knowledge and then denies it with his tongue, that denial does not make him an unbeliever, because knowledge does not disappear through denial. He therefore remains a believer.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01852
Al-Shahrastānī adds an important point. Speaking for Jahm, he says:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01853
“Faith cannot be divided.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01854
In other words, it cannot be broken down into belief, speech, and action.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01855
He then adds another statement from Jahm:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01856
“Nor do believers differ in the degree of their faith. The faith of the prophets and the faith of the community are of one kind, because knowledge itself does not differ in degree.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01857
Al-Baghdādī gives the same doctrine in essentially the same form.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01858
Opposite faith stands unbelief.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01859
So what, for Jahm, is unbelief?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01860
Al-Ashʿarī reports him as saying:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01861
“Unbelief is one single quality. It exists in the heart, and it is ignorance of God.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01862
We now have Jahm’s complete formula for faith and its opposite, unbelief.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01863
Faith is knowledge. Unbelief is ignorance.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01864
This is genuinely a new understanding of faith. It does not simply connect faith with knowledge. It makes the two the same thing.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01865

And if we remember that Jahm believed in knowledge reached through reason, and that he regarded reason as the first path to God even before revelation, then we can see that we are dealing with a new way of thinking.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01866

At this stage in the development of Arab-Islamic thought, we are beginning to reach a turning point. This new approach leads toward the rational and philosophical method later developed by the thinkers of kalām, which in turn helped prepare the way for the emergence of philosophy itself.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01867
One strong sign that this really was a turning point is the fierce opposition Jahm’s doctrine provoked among traditionalists.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01868
His rational method, whose main features we have now seen, seems to have been what most disturbed both the traditionalists and the Umayyad authorities.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01869

His determinism itself could fit quite comfortably with the ideology of Umayyad rule. But Jahm’s determinism was inseparable from the rational method he used to deal with the religious questions discussed above. As we have seen, he approached these questions with an unusual degree of independence and intellectual freedom.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01870
This bold rational tendency did not please the men who ruled the Umayyad state. On the contrary, it angered them.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01871

The class position of the Umayyad ruling order required its leaders to oppose firmly any intellectual movement that gave reason a place of its own, even a relatively independent one, outside the conservative “official” view of the state. Jahm had done precisely that.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01872

This may have been one of the factors that led him to answer the call of al-Ḥārith ibn Surayj in Khurasan. Near the end of Umayyad rule, Ibn Surayj called on Jahm to join his war against the Umayyads. Jahm did so, and both men were killed in 128 AH.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01873
There is another report that supports our interpretation.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01874
The Umayyad caliph Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik wrote to his representative in Khurasan, Naṣr ibn Sayyār:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01875
“A man named Jahm has appeared in your region, one of the Dahriyya.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01876
He then ordered:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01877
“If you capture him, kill him.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01878
Here Hishām accuses Jahm of belonging to the Dahriyya.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01879
Yet we find nothing in Jahm’s doctrine or recorded views that supports this accusation. Nor do we find even his fiercest opponents accusing him of it when they wrote against him.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01880

Tāj al-Dīn al-Subkī, for example, attacked Jahm harshly and strongly condemned his view of faith. Yet even al-Subkī said nothing to suggest that Jahm had left Islam. In fact, he tried to interpret Jahm’s position in a way that would keep him within an Islamic framework.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01881
Why, then, was the Umayyad ruler Hishām alone in attaching the charge of belonging to the Dahriyya to Jahm, and then using it as grounds for ordering his death?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01882
The answer clearly cannot be Jahm’s determinism.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01883
Determinism was itself one of the religious weapons used by the Umayyads to defend their political and class position.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01884

The more likely reason is that Jahm’s determinism existed alongside an intellectual independence from Umayyad “ideology.” It was also joined to the rational tendency that led him to give reason the leading role in dealing with some of the most sensitive religious questions of his time—questions closely tied to Islamic texts that still held the highest authority as sources of religious belief.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01885
This may be what Aḥmad Amīn meant in the statement we quoted earlier:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01886

“Although Jahm was a determinist, he nevertheless rebelled alongside those who rose against the Umayyads. He also held views that people strongly objected to. Politics exploited the public hostility toward him and killed him.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01887
We should not, however, overlook another factor when trying to understand the conflict between Jahm and the Umayyad authorities that ended in his death.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01888
Jahm was one of the mawālī. He grew up in a Persian environment in Khurasan and was attached as a client to a branch of the Arab tribe of Azd that lived there.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01889
He also spent part of his intellectual life in Kufa.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01890

Kufa was a place where thinkers and educated people from among the mawālī found room for political and intellectual activity against Umayyad rule. Their opposition came partly in response to the ethnic arrogance shown toward the mawālī by the Umayyad ruling order.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01891
It is quite possible that Jahm was influenced by this atmosphere, both politically and intellectually.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01892
There is another related point.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01893

Historians report that Jahm met al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham in Kufa. Al-Jaʿd was also one of the mawālī. They say that he had lived in Damascus, where the Umayyads became angry with him and pursued him, forcing him to flee to Kufa.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01894
According to these accounts, the reason for Umayyad anger was his belief that the Qurʾan was created. Al-Ṭabarī regarded him as the first person to make this claim, sometime after 120 AH.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01895

Taken together, all of this suggests that the environment of Kufa left both political and intellectual marks on Jahm. These influences may have helped shape some of his later positions toward the Umayyad state, as well as the Umayyad attitude toward him.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01896
Alongside this was the rational method that guided his independent thinking to its furthest conclusions.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01897
In the end, his life was brought to a close by political killing.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01898

As we come to the end of our discussion of Jahm ibn Ṣafwān, we should point to one final contradiction. It concerns Jahm’s historical role and the problems we face when trying to place him within the development of Arab-Islamic thought.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01899
The contradiction appears in the position of the traditionalists who opposed Jahm’s determinism.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01900
Most of the traditionalist writers who argued against him correctly identified a basic problem in his doctrine when they described it as “pure suspension.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01901
What they meant was that determinism makes religious duties meaningless.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01902

If human beings have no freedom of will in what they do, then there is little sense in commanding them to obey religious duties. Their obedience and disobedience do not come from their own will, but from a force that determines that will for them.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01903
Yet these same traditionalists also opposed the rational tendency on which Jahm’s entire system of thought was built.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01904
This created a contradiction within their own reasoning. From one side, opposing the independent use of reason ultimately leads toward opposing human freedom of will as well.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01905
Jahm fell into the opposite contradiction. His determinism conflicted, from another side, with the demands of the very rational approach on which his thought was based.
Summary of Chapter Two
en-s08-title
Summary of Chapter Two
Summary of Chapter Two
passage-en-01907
At the beginning of this chapter, we wanted to see how the fierce political struggle between the different Islamic parties and schools gradually became an intellectual struggle as well.
Summary of Chapter Two
passage-en-01908
One of the clearest signs of this change appeared in Islamic law. Two main approaches began to take shape: the school of reasoned judgment and the school of hadith.
Summary of Chapter Two
passage-en-01909

This division became increasingly clear and began to develop with some independence from the political conflict itself. The reason was that Islamic law was now facing new conditions created by the Arab conquests. Muslims were entering regions where social relations were very different from those they had known in Arabia when Islam first appeared. The conquests also forced the Islamic state to create new forms of organization.
Summary of Chapter Two
passage-en-01910
Islamic law therefore faced a new task. It had to deal with situations that had not existed before and develop new rulings for them, while still preserving the spirit of its general principles.
Summary of Chapter Two
passage-en-01911

This historical challenge showed just how necessary it was for law to develop as life itself developed. And it was only natural that people would differ over how far the law should change, just as they differed over change in the wider sense. In every age and every society, people have tended to divide according to their social positions between those who defend what already exists and those who seek to renew it.
Summary of Chapter Two
passage-en-01912
This was precisely the basis of the division among those concerned with Islamic law.
Summary of Chapter Two
passage-en-01913

The conservatives rejected rulings that had no explicit basis in the Qurʾan or the Sunna. The reformers, by contrast, used their own reasoned judgment to derive new rulings for questions that neither of these two main sources addressed. These questions had not existed in Arabian society when Islamic law first appeared. The reformers therefore used rational reasoning alongside the general principles of the law.
Summary of Chapter Two
passage-en-01914
From this division came two schools. The first became known as the People of Reasoned Judgment (Ahl al-Raʾy), and the second as the People of Hadith (Ahl al-Ḥadīth).
Summary of Chapter Two
passage-en-01915

The second of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, had in practice stood on the side of reasoned judgment during his caliphate. He made a number of rulings on his own judgment, and these later formed some of the earliest foundations of the school of raʾy.
Summary of Chapter Two
passage-en-01916

By the middle of the first Islamic century, this school had developed a clearer identity. It relied more heavily on independent judgment in matters of law and less heavily on hadith, especially after doubts had spread about the authenticity of many reports attributed to the Prophet.
Summary of Chapter Two
passage-en-01917

The other, more conservative school reacted strongly against this position. Some of its members went beyond simply rejecting reasoned judgment and independent legal interpretation. They also went so far in their use of hadith that some of them placed hadith above Qurʾanic texts.
Summary of Chapter Two
passage-en-01918
Even so, the school of reasoned judgment found many supporters in regions far from the Hijaz, where Islam had first appeared.
Summary of Chapter Two
passage-en-01919
This division eventually spread beyond questions of law. It became a wider intellectual division over many of the new problems created by the development of Arab-Islamic society.
Summary of Chapter Two
passage-en-01920

We therefore find many members of the school of reasoned judgment supporting an idea that emerged from the debate over divine decree and human action: the idea that human beings are free to choose their actions. Those who later became associated with this view were known as the Qadarites.
Summary of Chapter Two
passage-en-01921

Many followers of the hadith school, by contrast, supported the opposite view. They denied human freedom and held that every human action, good or bad, comes from God. Human beings, in other words, act under God’s decree and predestination. Those who later became known for this view were called the Jabriyya, or the advocates of compulsion.
Summary of Chapter Two
passage-en-01922

So each side in the legal debate—the conservatives on one side and the more forward-looking current on the other—moved naturally toward the side that best matched its outlook in this new intellectual struggle.
Summary of Chapter Two
passage-en-01923

We also saw in this chapter that the development of Arab-Islamic society during the early Islamic period—the age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs and the Umayyads—created the need for a broad cultural movement.
Summary of Chapter Two
passage-en-01924

This movement laid the basic foundations for organizing the different kinds of knowledge connected with Islam. These included the language of the Qurʾan and hadith, their literary style, their legal and moral teachings, and questions of belief. They also included the history of Islam itself: its preaching, its conquests, its leading figures, and its relationship with pre-Islamic Arab life in language, literature, history, customs, and traditions.
Summary of Chapter Two
passage-en-01925
Islam was the first and immediate starting point of this broad cultural movement.
Summary of Chapter Two
passage-en-01926
But once the basic rules for organizing this knowledge had been created in response to the needs of Islam, those same rules became the starting point for a wider cultural revival.
Summary of Chapter Two
passage-en-01927

Different branches of knowledge began to grow within it and gradually acquired some independence from one another. Each branch almost began to follow its own path. Their paths sometimes met, sometimes ran alongside one another, sometimes crossed, and sometimes joined together for a time before separating again.
Summary of Chapter Two
passage-en-01928
They continued to borrow from one another—material, examples, methods, and teaching practices—but this did not remove the relative independence that each field gradually developed.
Summary of Chapter Two
passage-en-01929
This independence did not become fully clear until the end of the second Islamic century.
Summary of Chapter Two
passage-en-01930

In this way there emerged what came to be known as the “Arabic sciences”: language, grammar, rhetoric, history, biography, Qurʾanic interpretation, hadith, and the study of the transmitters of hadith. Then came the sciences connected with poetry: metre, rhyme, classifications of poets, comparisons between them, the transmission of poetry, commentaries on poetry, and so on.
